about: The officeholder's day (OFFICE-LOCAL): when a local body meets, how long it sits, and what stops the player by default.

eveningMeetingMinute.source: A city council or town board's regular meeting starts in the evening, about 6:00 p.m., so members who hold day jobs can sit (published meeting schedules cited in data/research/local-government/council-meeting-intervals.json: Cupertino, Waco, Willis, the Michigan townships meet at 6:00 to 7:00 p.m.).

daytimeMeetingMinute.source: A county board's regular meeting starts in the morning, about 9:00 a.m. (county commissions commonly sit at 9:00 to 10:00 a.m. on a weekday; Texas commissioners courts and Georgia county commissions publish morning sessions).

meetingMinutes.source: How long a regular local meeting sits, call to order to adjournment. Cupertino's analysis of council meetings 2017 to 2024 counts meetings averaging about two to three hours; small boards often adjourn in under two.

meetingWeekday.source: The weekday a body's regular meeting falls on, 0 Sunday to 6 Saturday, until the place's own rule is read: Tuesday, the day most of the cited councils and boards use. A place's recorded rule replaces it.

agendaNoticeDays.source: How many days before a regular meeting its agenda is posted, after which a new item waits for the next meeting. State open-meetings laws commonly require 24 to 72 hours' public notice of a regular meeting's agenda (for example California's Brown Act, Gov. Code sec. 54954.2, 72 hours; Texas Gov. Code sec. 551.043, 72 hours).

fullTimeWeeklyHours.source: Full-time work is 35 hours or more a week (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey definitions). A seat whose estimated hours reach it is the holder's job.

deskMinute.source: When a bill that passed reaches the executive's desk: the next working morning, 9:00 a.m., when the clerk's transmittal is read. The office's own signing deadline (the legislature engine) is unchanged.
